newsitem.title: CHINA: China PM's speech shows importance of markets.
newsitem.headline: China PM's speech shows importance of markets.

text.p: The call by Chinese Premier Li Peng for continued regulation of China's fledgling securities and futures markets shows the importance the Beijing government attaches to their development, analysts said on Sunday.
"There used to be a concern that China's stock and futures markets would be closed after Deng Xiaoping died," said an analyst in Shanghai with Guotai Securities Co, a major brokerage.
"But now there is no question of that happening," he said.
In his annual government work report to the National People's Congress, or parliament, on Saturday, Li called for continued regulation of China's futures and securities markets.
"We must regulate the securities and futures market and increase our sense of risk," he said.

While his stand on the markets offered little shift from a three-year crackdown, the official Shanghai Securities News said on Sunday it was the first mention in a government work report of China's stock and futures markets and indicated the government would stick with current economic policies.
"It showed the position and function of the securities markets has become more promiment in China's economy as a whole," it said of Li's speech.
"It also indicated the government takes seriously and is determined to solve the problems existing in the development of the securities and futures markets," the newspaper said.

The forward-looking reform policies of Deng Xiaoping, China's paramount leader for 18 years until his death last month, took China from an impoverished, backward nation to one of the world's fastest growing economies.
Analysts regard the opening in the early 1990s of stock and futures markets in major Chinese cities as a major thrust of Deng's aim of integrating China's economy with the rest of the world.
The Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges opened in 1990, and futures markets in these and several other cities opened in 1992.

Because the markets remain in their infancy, there have been widespread irregularities, including institutional manipulation, listed companies trading their own shares, and credit trading on the primary stock market, all of which are illegal, another Chinese analyst said.
Uncovering these illegal practices has taxed the energy of China's regulatory bodies, and is seen as necessary if the markets are to mature with any credibility, he said.
"Regulation has been the key-note for the markets for a long time now and that situation will continue," another analyst, with Shenyin-Wanguo Securities, said.
The China Securities Regulatory Commission, the country's top securities watchdog, has taken a series of steps to regulate the markets.
The Saturday edition of Shanghai Securities News reported the banning by the Commission of three trading houses for manipulating red bean futures prices on the Tianjin United Futures Exchange.
"China's stock markets are relatively standardised, but there are more problems on the futures markets," the Guotai analyst said.
He said Li's words were unlikely to move markets on Monday, but did indicate the government's desire for their stable development.
